hints: Focus on what a positively charged intermediate means here, a carbocation formed when the C-Br bond breaks first.
Classify each bromoalkane by looking at the carbon holding Br, count how many other carbons are attached to it to find primary versus tertiary.
Remember that tertiary carbocations are the most stable, so the tertiary bromoalkane is the one that will favour the SN1 route through a carbocation.
walkthrough:
**Recall the two hydrolysis mechanisms**

Warm dilute NaOH(aq) replaces Br with OH by nucleophilic substitution. This can happen by SN1 or SN2.

SN1 route with carbocation:
$$\text{R-Br} \rightarrow \text{R}^{+} + \text{Br}^{-} \text{ then } \text{R}^{+} + \text{OH}^{-} \rightarrow \text{R-OH}$$

**Classify each bromoalkane**

Look at the C atom bonded to Br. If it is joined to only one other carbon, it is primary. If joined to three other carbons, it is tertiary.

$\text{1-bromopentane}$: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{Br}$, primary. $\text{1-bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane}$: $(\text{CH}_{3})_{3}\text{CCH}_{2}\text{Br}$, primary. $\text{1-bromo-3-methylbutane}$: primary. $\text{2-bromo-2-methylbutane}$: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{C(Br)(CH}_{3}\text{)CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, tertiary.

**Link carbocation stability to mechanism**

SN1 needs a stable carbocation intermediate. Stability order is tertiary > secondary > primary because alkyl groups donate electron density.

Only the tertiary bromoalkane forms a stable enough $\text{R}^{+}$ to go SN1 readily, so it is most likely to involve a positively charged intermediate.

options.A: 1-bromopentane is a primary bromoalkane. It forms a very unstable primary carbocation, so it reacts mainly by SN2 with no carbocation intermediate in one concerted step.
options.B: 1-bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane is also primary at the C-Br carbon, despite being branched elsewhere. It cannot form a stable carbocation directly and is even hindered for SN2, but it does not favour a simple SN1 carbocation.
options.C: 1-bromo-3-methylbutane is primary. Like other primary haloalkanes, it prefers SN2 attack by OH- and does not form a positively charged intermediate.
options.D: 2-bromo-2-methylbutane is tertiary. Loss of Br- gives a stable tertiary carbocation, $(CH3)2C+CH2CH3$, so hydrolysis proceeds readily by SN1 via this positively charged intermediate.
